svg.title: OSPF and IS-IS compared across seven dimensions, with the selection guidance
svg.desc: Seven comparison rows. Extensibility: OSPF uses LSAs with fixed formats and needs new types, IS-IS uses type-length-value fields so new capabilities are added without a new protocol version. Hierarchy: OSPF uses areas with a mandatory backbone that must touch area 0, IS-IS uses levels with level-2 continuous and no separate backbone area. Running over IP: OSPF runs over IP protocol 89 and needs IP reachability first, IS-IS runs directly over layer 2 with protocol 124, so it can route before IP is up. Migration: OSPF is easier to migrate and has broader vendor support and more people know it; IS-IS is harder to understand and has fewer trained engineers. Segment routing: IS-IS with wide metrics has become the common choice in large service provider cores, OSPF supports it but is less common there. Vendor reality: OSPF is present everywhere; IS-IS is present on most but not on all low-end platforms. The verdict is that complexity is not the deciding factor, operational familiarity is; and given equal capability, choose the one the team can troubleshoot at three in the morning.
svg.text: OSPF and IS-IS compared on the seven dimensions that actually decide it
The differences are real, but only two of them change an outcome at most enterprises
DIMENSION
OSPF
IS-IS
Extensibility
LSAs have fixed formats; a new capability
usually means a new LSA type or a new version.
TLV-based: new capability = new sub-TLV, no new
protocol version, and unknown TLVs are ignored safely.
Hierarchy
Areas with a mandatory backbone; every non-
backbone area must touch area 0.
Levels 1 and 2; level-2 is contiguous and needs no
separate backbone area. Fewer constraints, stricter nodes.
Runs over
IP protocol 89 — needs IP reachability before it
can build adjacencies.
Layer 2 directly, protocol 124 — it can route
before IP is up, which is why it suits transport networks.
Migration and skills
Broader support, easier to migrate to, more
people on the market already know it.
Harder to learn (NSAP addressing, levels), fewer
engineers, so the training cost is real and ongoing.
Segment routing
Supported, but less common in large cores.
Wide metrics are needed for the larger label space.
The common choice for large service provider cores:
wide metric plus TLV extension, and it is already layer 2 native.
Platform coverage
Available essentially everywhere, down to
small switches and firewalls.
Present on most platforms, but not all — verify the
low-end model before standardising on it.
Troubleshooting
Readable LSDB and neighbour states; the output
maps onto how people describe the network.
The LSP and TLV model is less intuitive at first,
but the database is flat and predictable once learned.
The honest verdict: only two rows usually change an enterprise outcome — platform coverage and the skills already on the team.
TLV extensibility matters at service provider scale and in segment routing cores; it does not matter in a 300-router campus.
Given similar capability, choose the protocol the on-call engineer can troubleshoot at 3 a.m. That is an engineering criterion, not a political one.
